speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: On behalf of the Minister for Home Affairs, I beg to move, "That the Bill be now read a Second time".

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Secret societies have been in Singapore for a long time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In the 1950s, gang activity in Singapore was rampant.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Secret societies were involved in illicit activities and used violence to impose fear on the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Victims and witnesses feared reprisal against themselves and their family members, if they testified against the secret societies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It was against this backdrop that the Act was introduced.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Act gave the Government levers to deal effectively with the problem.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Under the Act, the Minister for Home Affairs may detain, or place under Police supervision, persons associated with activities of a criminal nature.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These activities are set out in the Fourth Schedule of the Act and include involvement in a secret society or as a gangster.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Minister must be satisfied that detaining a person under the Act is necessary in the interests of public safety, peace and good order.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The power to detain someone under the Act is used only when prosecution is not viable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, because victims and witnesses refuse to testify for fear of reprisal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We have put in place safeguards in the exercise of these powers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, the consent of the Public Prosecutor must be obtained for a detention order or supervision order.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: He must be satisfied that prosecution is not viable, before allowing executive action under the Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, we have three committees that are independent of the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) to ensure that detentions are necessary in the interests of public safety, peace and good order.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The first committee scrutinises every detention and supervision order issued by the Minister.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It is chaired by a sitting Judge of the Supreme Court and comprises senior and experienced lawyers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It examines the evidence that was considered by the Minister in issuing the order and submits its report to the President to recommend the confirmation, variation or cancellation of the order.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A second committee considers every confirmed detention order at least once annually.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It will consider whether the detainee continues to pose a threat to public safety, peace and good order; and whether the detainee should continue to be detained or released.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: A third committee reviews detention cases which are being considered for extension beyond 10 years, to determine if continued detention is indeed necessary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Act requires the committees to have regard to public safety, the protection of individuals and the safeguarding of sources of information, in their deliberation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They are required to submit a report to the President, who may, on the advice of the Cabinet, confirm, vary or cancel the order made by the Minister.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Third, detainees are required to attend in person before the first committee, when the committee considers the order made by the Minister.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Detainees can be represented by lawyers and may make representations to the various committees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Fourth, every decision made under the Act can be subject to judicial review.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This was made clear by the Minister for Home Affairs when the Act was amended in 2018.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Over the years, the number of detention and supervision orders issued under the Act has declined.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This was fewer than the number of cases in the same period of the previous term of the Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Gangs and organised crime groups continue to be a big threat to societies globally.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These groups are involved in a wide spectrum of criminal conduct, including illegal drugs, scams, money laundering, human trafficking, firearms and vehicle-related crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In the United States (US), gangs and gang-related criminal activities remain prevalent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Gangs there actively recruit new members, have carved out drug distribution territories and collaborate with other criminal groups for power and financial gains.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They are well-organised and have significant reach and influence even across the US borders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In August 2023, the United Nations reported that hundreds of thousands of people are being trafficked by criminal gangs and coerced into working in scam centres and other illegal operations across Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Billions of dollars are made annually by such gangs, who force the victims into crime and subject them to threats, torture and even sexual violence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There is a strong nexus between gang membership and violent crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Studies have found that gangs reinforce violent behaviour by routinely exposing gang members to high-risk situations and rewarding them for their violence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Moreover, gang members often see violence as a way to earn respect, status and reputation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Because of the way gangs operate, witness intimidation in gang trials is a serious concern for many jurisdictions and an obstacle to justice.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The true extent of this is impossible to measure, because witness intimidation is often not reported.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In a recent incident in Virginia, US, a member of a street gang intimidated witnesses by posting their names on Instagram and calling for gang members to gather in the court room to “watch the snitches snitching”.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As a result, some witnesses pulled out of testifying and the trial had to be postponed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: When criminals, such as gangs and secret societies, cannot be brought to justice for their crimes, then the criminal justice system has failed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Instead of the people feeling protected, a climate of fear envelopes the society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The people lose confidence in the criminal justice system and, ultimately, the state.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As I explained earlier, the Act is used where prosecution is not viable, because witnesses are unwilling to testify in court for fear of reprisal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Witness intimidation is a problem in Singapore too.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Some countries have witness relocation and protection programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, because Singapore is so small, witness relocation would not be feasible or effective.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Even in big countries, these measures are not always foolproof.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Moreover, witness protection programmes take a very heavy toll on the protected witnesses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They have to change their identity, change their job and cut off contact with families and friends.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We should ask ourselves: why should witnesses and victims have to bear heavy personal costs, in bringing secret society members to justice?

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In Singapore, there are still active secret societies, although not in the numbers and scale in some other countries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Nevertheless, they are still a menace to law and order, public safety and security.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They recruit young Singaporeans, and engage in illicit activities and violent conduct.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: That is why we must continue to clamp down on them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I will give you a few recent examples of when we had to use the powers under the Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Ten gang members gathered at a rival gang member’s flat.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They were armed with deadly weapons including a machete, a knuckle duster and a karambit knife.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They were there to seek revenge as they believed that a rival gang member had assaulted their "Headman".

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: When they found out that the rival gang member was not at home, they attacked his family members instead.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They punched and kicked the person’s parents, brother and sister.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The father suffered a facial bone fracture while the mother sustained a forearm fracture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Another incident took place on 8 January 2022 at about 10.30 pm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There was a gang clash between rival secret societies at Circular Road.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: During the riot, gang members of one of the secret societies chased and assaulted the rival gang members.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The rival gang members were kicked and punched in full view of the public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: One gang member used a knife to stab a rival gang member’s leg.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Four of the gang members were dealt with under the Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In addition to gang-related incidents, the Act is also used against organised crimes such as unlicensed moneylending.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Without the Act, we would not have been able to do much against them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The victims and witnesses feared reprisal and were not willing to testify.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The perpetrators would have been able to carry on with their violence and intimidation with impunity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We cannot be complacent about the safety and security that Singaporeans enjoy today, that we do not live in fear of gangs and secret societies and are not intimidated by them, unlike in many other countries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Act is an essential tool for the Government to ensure this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This Bill represents the 15th time that Parliament is being asked to extend the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given the longevity of this Act, which was enacted almost 70 years ago, the skeptical amongst us may be tempted to say that there is nothing "temporary" about this Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would respectfully suggest, however, that that would be a case of missing the wood for the trees.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This Act vests with the Minister for Home Affairs with extraordinary powers to order the detention without trial of a person accused of having association with specified activities of a criminal nature, DO, or subjecting him to a supervision order, or SO.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These powers are meant to be used as a matter of last resort because of the difficulty in securing evidence against such persons, as explained by the hon Minister of State; primarily by reason of their association with secret societies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: By design, these powers constitute a derogation from the usual due process accorded to persons accused of crime which will involve the court independently adjudicating on the case after reviewing the evidence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The exception has been justified on the basis of the pernicious nature of secret society operations and the need to preserve public order in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As was mentioned by the hon Minister of State, several safeguards have also been worked into the framework as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, I would not traverse the same ground save to add that in respect of the Advisory Committees the hon Minister of State mentioned are headed by sitting Judges of the Supreme Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, all of them are occupying a high constitutional office.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Notwithstanding the safeguards, given the exceptional nature of the power, however, it is apt that there is a further mechanism built into the Act to allow Parliament to satisfy itself of the continued need to confer on the Minister these powers before deciding to extend the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, the reference to "temporary" in the Act is really a recognition of the fact that these are extraordinary powers requiring the Minister to periodically make a case in Parliament on the reasons for extending the Act to enable him to use the powers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to the hon Minister of State’s case for extending the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For context, these detention numbers were much higher in the 1980s and up to the early 1990s, they were in the four digits and they were in the three digits up to the first decade of the new millennium.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, it is therefore good news that the numbers have reduced appreciably over the past four decades.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The bad news, however, as I note from the hon Minister of State’s speech, is that there continues to be a number of serious secret society clashes that affect the peace and good order of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is noteworthy is that prosecution in these cases, as was mentioned by the hon Minister of State, was not viable because witnesses refused to give evidence in court, for fear of reprisal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such violent acts, should they have gone unpunished, would threaten the peace and security we are accustomed to, and some even take for granted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In addition, the hon Minister of State refers to a significant number organised criminal activities such as unlicensed moneylending and drug trafficking by secret societies again where witnesses are unwilling to come forward to testify incident in court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Without the decisive action taken under this Act to cripple the syndicates, many more Singaporeans may have fallen victim.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, hence, this Act had the effect of preventing the proliferation of such crime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would imagine them to be fairly sophisticated in their criminal activities and it would likely not be easy to get witnesses to spill the beans on them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This brings to my mind what the then Minister for Home Affairs, Mr Wong Kan Seng said in this House in 1994, about the threat of organised crime, particularly Asian triads and gangs, which continues to be real across much of the world today too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Wong stated that the Act served as a deterrence against these overseas triads and gangs from shifting operations into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To deal with these hardened criminals with sophisticated international networks, we need laws with teeth and muscle.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Through my pro bono criminal law practice as well as a two-year involvement in a study of youths at risk for a self-help group, I have noted the tendency for secret societies to recruit youths from a relatively young age: young people are the "oxygen" or life blood for secret societies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Once recruited, the youths become the secret societies' fighters who protect and advance their criminal objectives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I will be alluding to shortly, if we can starve the secret societies of this "oxygen", we will be able to significantly curb the societies' influence and activities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Once these youths join the secret societies, a number of them would be introduced to alcohol and controlled drugs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They in turn develop violent streaks which the headmen would then use to unleash against rival gangs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, I was personally involved in a pro bono case where a 17-year-old boy was issued with a DO which was subsequently extended as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the face of it, I would imagine that for some of us, this may be seen as a case of using a sledgehammer to crack a nut.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, the reality is that, depending on the facts of the case, young people, as part of a gang, can cause serious harm; even death.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They pose a danger to themselves too as violence begets violence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Depending on the facts, it may be necessary to invoke the Act to issue either a DO or SO to preserve public safety, peace and good order in Singapore, something we cannot take for granted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am aware that the Police does good work to help youths to keep away from the clutches of secret societies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister, in his answer to my PQ in 2020 highlighted some of these steps.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said that the Police works with the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF), Ministry of Education (MOE) and Singapore Prison Service (SPS) to develop and implement preventive and rehabilitative initiatives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These initiatives include the Streetwise and Enhanced Streetwise Programmes aimed at providing youths associated with secret societies with counselling.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Secret Societies Branch of the Criminal Investigation Department also regularly runs Camps ACE, which means "All Can Escape" to educate youths on the perils of joining a secret society and educational talks for parents on tell-tale signs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, the secret societies are not keeping still.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Through my work in the study, I learnt that secret societies have evolved methods to specifically target and recruit youths in communities and school settings as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These societies may well double their efforts in an environment where, generally, enrolment in secret societies is falling.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The activities usually start off as being rather innocuous social gatherings but lead to initiation ceremonies after which the youths would start being at the beck and call of their respective headmen.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I see such recruitment activities as "capacity building" to undertake activities of a criminal nature that are contemplated under the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such acts should equally be viewed as affecting the peace and good order of Singapore too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am aware that recruiting persons to join unlawful societies constitute an offence under the Societies Act 1966.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Where the Police has secured evidence of recruitment activities, such persons should be prosecuted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In cases where the evidence on record is not forthcoming, perhaps because of intimidation, I wonder if the powers under the Act can also be invoked against these recruiters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In paragraph 3 of the Fourth Schedule to the Act, which the hon Minister of State quoted, the Minister may use his power to detain a person or subject him to supervision if the person is generally involved in a secret society or as a gangster.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This should extend to recruitment activities on behalf of a secret society or gang.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, I seek the hon Minister of State’s clarification and views on this matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The final point I wish to make concerns the provisions in Parts 2, 3 and 4 of the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is not well known that the Act does not just deal with detention and supervision powers which are set out in Part 5 of the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because at almost every Second Reading debate of the Bill to extend the Act, the Government made its case by reference to its report card of the use of powers provided for in Part 5 of the Act; not Parts 2, 3 and 4.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such a move would be more in accord with Parliament’s intent when passing this Bill to extend the Act for a further five years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Going down to some specifics, Part 3 of the Act deals with placing prohibitions and restrictions on the ability of workers to strike and employers to lock-out workmen when they are engaged in "essential services" which is defined in the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The International Labour Organization, of which Singapore is a member of, expressly acknowledged that there may be a prohibition or restriction to the right to strike in essential services.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I therefore suggest that the Government consider taking steps to port Part 3 of the Act over to another statute, perhaps the Industrial Relations Act 1960.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Parts 2 and 4 of the Act deal with public safety and public order issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For instance, in section 4 under Part 2 of the Act, it is provided that any person who has a "subversive document", as defined in the Act, shall be guilty of an offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Section 13 under Part 4 of the Act provides the power to the Minister and the Police to disperse assemblies which pose an immediate threat to public peace.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I suggest that the Government reviewing these Parts with a view to repeal provisions that may be seen as obsolete or otiose.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Young people are not just the life blood of secret societies but of our country too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Once our young get snared into the gangs, their future prospects will naturally suffer.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Needless to say, their families suffer together with them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This law puts people behind bars or restricts their movement at the order of the Home Affairs Minister.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Like the Internal Security Act, it is a controversial exception to our legal justice system, which usually requires every person to be charged, tried and convicted in Court before he is imprisoned or fined for his wrongdoing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Minister can also make an order for a person to be subject to the supervision of the Police for any period not exceeding three years, if he is satisfied that it is so necessary.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Every order shall be referred to an advisory committee, which shall submit its recommendation on the order to the President, who has the power to confirm, cancel or vary the order given.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Taking away someone's liberty either by detention or by restriction of movements and activities should not be taken lightly as they impact on liberty and freedom.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Time limits for detention and supervision should also be viewed from the perspective that each order can be reviewed annually with the agreement of the President and that the recommendation of an advisory committee and on the advice of the Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am glad that we are here today to debate the extension of the Act for another five years and not more than that.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the past, some Members have even suggested that the Bill should not be a temporary one but should be converted to a permanent one.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many Members have, over the years, also spoken in agreement with the Minister of the day on variously the rationale for extending the Act to deal with the concerned crimes or criminal groups of the day.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I read from Ministers' and Members' speeches in the Hansard that this ranged from secret societies, gangsterism, drug trafficking, murders, extortion and protection records to, in more recent years, money laundering, loan-shark syndicates, organised crimes and global match-fixing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There was also mention of arguably activities which are traditionally not regarded as criminal, such as prevention of strikes and lockouts, as well as communist domination.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can the Minister of State give a breakdown of the number of persons subject to CLTPA orders, organised according to the different category of criminal activities?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can the Minister of State tell this House of the persons who have been detained in the course of the last five years, what is the proportion of detainees who have served more than two years and how many of the current detainees have been in detention for more than five and 10 years respectively?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister of State, in the past five years, whether there were instances when the public prosecutor actually withheld consent or raised concerns when the Minister sought to make an order.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Among other things, in 2018, the Workers' Party had expressed concern with the finality clause in the amended section 30 of the present Act under the then clause 3 of the Amendment Bill, which made the decisions of the Minister on detention and supervision to be final, the insertion of the Fourth Schedule which may allow Minister to bypass answering questions, such as whether a case is serious enough to justify detention, or why it is not possible to prosecute these persons in Court and also expanding the Minister's powers to police criminal activities overseas.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I confirm that the Workers' Party objections and reservations to some of the amendments raised in 2018 remain.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, we are in cautious support for the proposed five-year extension today, subject to the Government's explanation for the Authority's use of the CLTPA in the past five years and justifications for an extension of a further five years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He mentioned of victims being unwilling or unable to identify attackers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He also mentioned of victims or drug couriers unwilling to testify in Court for fear of reprisals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Minister also mentioned that while the drug situation was under control, the challenges had remained significant.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The same release also provided four recent cases of CLTPA recent enforcement, all involving gangs and witnesses refusing to give evidence for fear of reprisal.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Minister of State has also briefly touched on this in his speech.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Indeed, the scenario shared by the Minister then and the Minister of State today are not new and CLTPA has been used in such cases relating to crime and drug syndicates and gangs for a long time and they would often involve fear of witnesses testifying in Court for fear of reprisals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Looking at the explanations given and the cases mentioned by the Minister in the recent Second Reading speeches, I do wonder whether the Government will require further extensions of the Act as long as criminal activities, such as gangs, drug and crime syndicates, unlicensed moneylending and so on, continue to persist, especially coupled with possible intimidation of witnesses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How has Singapore Police Force (SPF) utilised the technological advances and deployment of technology in the Police Force, for example, use of cameras at an unprecedented scale these days to keep these crimes problems under control?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Indeed, with the increased use of technology by our SPF and also the development of SPF over the years, will advances in our policing methods as well as technological advances help to control the age-old problems of gangs and crime syndicates and mitigate against the age-old problem of witnesses not coming forth to testify?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Over time, other Members have also asked the question essentially of when we will be ready to do away with the Act.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The current Minister of Home Affairs has asked a similar question even back in 1989.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Almost 35 years on, I look forward to the current Minister's answer and update.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This extension is not to be taken lightly because it continues to empower the Government to detain individuals without trial.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Bill was first introduced in Parliament back in 1955, as one of the measures to counter the communist threat in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the most concerning part of the Act, namely the section empowering the Minister to direct a person to be detained without trial, was introduced in 1958 to deal with gangsterism.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the Second Reading of that amendment Bill, the Chief Secretary then, Mr EB David said, “It is only the exceptional gravity of the present state of gang lawlessness, which compels the Government to seek these exceptional powers for immediate use.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: No democratic government will lightly curtail the liberty of any individual by executive action, nor would it wish to curtail that liberty for a moment longer than is absolutely necessary.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the slowly increasing mutual confidence between the police and the public, I sincerely hope that it would not be very long before the conditions in which these gangsters can flourish will no longer obtain.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The normal processes of law will, once more, be adequate to detect and punish crimes and these special powers can be thankfully surrendered.” This Act was enacted in 1955 and if it is renewed this time, it would be its 15th renewal.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sixty-six years have passed since the introduction of the provision empowering the Executive to detain criminals without trial.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While gangsterism still exists today in Singapore, the extent of lawlessness is, we believe, not as rampant as it was back in 1958 when the executive power to detain without trial was introduced.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The most important question which we face today in this House is whether the Act is still relevant, and more importantly, necessary in light of our present circumstances.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This consideration must include other pieces of criminal legislation in force and the sufficiency and efficacy of our judicial system.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A balance has to be struck between personal liberty and public peace and order.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Have we struck the right balance with this proposed extension?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As such, the Progress Singapore Party (PSP) would like to seek several clarifications from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, does the Ministry intend to continually renew this piece of legislation for as long as crime in Singapore is not completely eradicated?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Otherwise, can the Ministry share with this House under what circumstances it is prepared to do away with this piece of legislation, which was intended to be temporary when it was first enacted in 1955?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, can the Ministry update this House regarding the steps it has taken over the years to review if our current judicial system can be strengthened to better deal with crimes of the nature that this Act is currently invoked for, without having to detain persons without trial?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Three, can the Minister clarify whether the Public Defender's Office is authorised to represent detainees under the Act to guarantee their access to counsel?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, as the powers given to the Government under the CLTPA is so draconian, PSP is of the view that equally strong safeguards must be put in place to protect innocent Singaporeans against any potential abuse of these powers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We, therefore, propose to enhance the protections against possible abuse with three recommendations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we note that Minister Shanmugam said in 2018 that Advisory Committees will be chaired by sitting judges of the Supreme Court of Singapore, the Government stopped short of codifying this change.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSP is of the view that we must codify this requirement to uphold the separation of powers, provide greater clarity for all and strengthen the perception that the Advisory Committees are independent.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that there is no downside to this.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSP's second proposed safeguard relates to the making of DOs and PSO.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSP's third proposed safeguard relates to the extension of DOs or PSOs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reason why we are proposing the second and third safeguards is because the ultimate decision-maker, currently, is still Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the Minister must hear the Advisory Committee's views and recommendations via its written report to the President, the Minister does not need to follow those recommendations before making or renewing the DO or PSO, since the President does not have discretionary powers under the CLTPA and must follow Cabinet's recommendations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSP believes that these three proposals will strike the appropriate balance between personal liberty and public peace and order.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also recognise the CLTPA's role in keeping Singapore safe.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we also recognise that our circumstances have changed substantially since the enactment of the CLTPA in the 1950s and that detention without trial must always be considered with utmost caution and reluctance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should also clarify our laws and codify the current practices that are already in place.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will take the Chair at 3.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When I last spoke on the Bill to renew the CLTPA, I said that the title of the Bill belies the fact that the Act is far from temporary.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The debate that we are having today on extending the CLPTA is an important safeguard.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This ensures that there is Parliamentary scrutiny on the continuing need for the Executive’s exceptional powers under the CLPTA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While I understand the continuing public order and security pressures that justify the exercise of these powers, we should never forget the extraordinary nature of the CLTPA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The grounds for the Act and the powers under the CLPTA should be closely examined every time the Act comes up for renewal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the previous amendment, the obligations on a person subject to a Police Supervision Order were moved into subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The obligations are now set out under rules that the Minister can make under section 49.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister shared that the rationale for doing so was to allow the obligations, which are operational in nature, to be amended based on evolving needs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State share the nature of these obligations that have been introduced in the rules?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How frequently are the obligations reviewed and how have they evolved since the previous amendment to the Act?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the composition and processes of the Advisory Committees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Advisory Committee, which reviews DOs and PSOs, is chaired by a Judge of the Supreme Court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Its members are senior lawyers and respected members of society, such as Justices of the Peace.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Advisory Committee will consider all materials that the Minister relied on in issuing the DO or PSO.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The compositions of the other two types of Advisory Committees are not as clear.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State share the composition of the other two Advisory Committees which review existing detainees’ cases at least once annually and for extension beyond 10 years?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As these two Advisory Committees must consider the detainee’s suitability and readiness for release, can Minister share whether there are professionals on the Advisory Committees who have the relevant expertise?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, the Advisory Committee may have to take a view on the detainee’s psychological state or receptiveness to rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, section 40(3) also requires the Advisory Committees to consider the requirements of public safety, the protection of individuals and the safeguarding of sources of information.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State share what materials are provided to the two Advisory Committees that review existing detainees’ cases to enable them to consider all these factors?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State also share whether the two Advisory Committees that review existing detainees’ cases regularly exercise their powers under section 40 to summon and examine witnesses, and to compel the production of documents?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is on the support of individuals subjected to DOs and PSOs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry has stated that DOs and PSOs are intended to “break the vicious cycle of gang lawlessness and the climate of terror they instilled”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In order to break this vicious cycle, can the Minister of State share what programmes are in place for individuals subject to DOs and PSOs to reduce the need for the DOs or PSOs to be extended?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My fourth and final point is on witness protection.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I suggested in my speech on the previous amendments to the Act that the Ministry should study other solutions for securing witness testimony to reduce the need for the CLTPA powers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Minister of State shared that the suggestions considered were not workable because it is difficult to have secret testimony from one witness who cannot be cross-examined in the trial process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the Minister of State also said that the Ministry will review other options for securing witness testimonies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State provide an update on its review and options that were considered?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act, which I will now refer to simply as "the Act", has been in place since 1955, and contains several provisions relating to public safety and security in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: These issues are important, and need to be acknowledged and seriously considered prior to approval of this Bill; and I will now make some additional comments intended to assist these considerations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Before I do so, I would like to note that I am currently Head of the Public Safety and Security Programme at Singapore University of Social Sciences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act 1955 was initially intended to combat crimes, notably violent conflicts, between gangs and secret societies, and to ensure the uninterrupted provision of essential services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The criminal landscape in Singapore has, however, changed and Singapore now ranks as one of the safest countries in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We also now have an independent and impartial judiciary, highly trained and respected police and security forces, and a population that is known around the world as being law abiding and civic minded.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Why then, do we need such powers as contained in the Act?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While crime rates across Singapore remain admirably low by international standards, we continue to face the threat of national and transnational crime that is increasingly sophisticated, complex and elusive, and can have far reaching consequences on the personal and economic safety and wellbeing of individual citizens and the nation as a whole.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, our low crimes rates do not just spontaneously happen.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: They are the result of the coordinated and continual efforts of many hundreds of thousands of Singaporeans who work often invisibly every day to keep us safe, and who are backed up by legislation that gives them the authority and confidence to do what they need to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As Thomas Jefferson famously said, "the price of freedom is eternal vigilance", and while this Act may curtail or impede certain individual rights and freedoms, it does assist to guarantee the collective freedom and well-being of Singapore and Singaporeans – something many of us take for granted every day and would complain loudly about if it was to vanish.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In comparison to almost all other countries, Singapore is tiny, with a population density that is third highest in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The impact of crime in Singapore is not the same as that in other countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: If our crime rates increase, they cannot be hidden or distributed across large geographical areas, or within dispersed population groups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: An escalation in crime in Singapore will literally, be in our face, and the impact of that crime on the efficiency, cooperation, and trust that drives Singapore could be catastrophic on our society, our economy, and our reputation as a uniquely safe place to live, work and invest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: To counter these misconceptions, it might be helpful for the Government to run a public education campaign about how and when the provisions in the Act are applied, and the checks and balances that exist within our systems to ensure that the provisions are applied transparently and appropriately and only ever as a last resort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It may also be helpful to remind the public that those who are detained are able to seek legal advice and appeal to the relevant Advisory Committee or Courts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate the challenges explained by the hon Minister of State earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, if more could be done to reassure witnesses that their identity and safety is guaranteed, then perhaps more of these cases could be successfully prosecuted through our regular court system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, if another justification for detention under the Act is the difficulty in obtaining reliable evidence, I would also welcome clarification about the existence and use of confidential disclosure or whistleblowing schemes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: If more people were able to easily and confidentially provide evidence to the authorities, then perhaps they would be more willing and able to submit, or even leak relevant information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: These suggestions may be of particular relevance in those matters involving organised crime syndicates or gangs, or where witnesses or evidence may not be based in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: First, it removes the opportunity for offenders to commit further crimes, and, of equal, if not more, importance, it provides an opportunity to rehabilitate offenders so as to facilitate successful reintegration into society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: That is, as well as initially removing these alleged offenders from society, are they also being successfully rehabilitated and reintegrated back into the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Related to this issue is the gang membership.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: If this is the case, and gang related activity remains a primary reason for detention, I would welcome clarification about whether those detained under the Act have access to programmes specifically targeting issues surrounding gang membership.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This is a major issue of concern, and we need to examine and address why so many people in Singapore, including young people, still feel the need to join or be affiliated with a gang.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: If we can intervene early in the lives of young people and provide them with access to more constructive and positive social networking options, we could perhaps start to break the ongoing cycle of gang related crime.
It is a unique sunset clause, which states that the law continues in force for period of five years.
This means that the law will lapse at the end of five years, unless it is renewed by Parliament at today's Second Reading.
The arguments for retaining this Bill in our statutes have been put forth and debated on many, many occasions in this House.

The essence of this law is that allows the Minister to detain a person who has been associated with activities of a criminal nature, without having to charge that person or bring him to trial, if the Minister is satisfied that the detention is an interest of public safety, peace and good order.
The Minister also has similar powers to order a person to be subject to a supervision of the Police.
And in this Act, activities of a criminal nature means any activity specified in the fourth schedule.

In previous debates, the Minister for Home Affairs had listed the situations when the Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act was applied, firstly, against gang-related criminal activities; second, against drug traffickers; third, against unlicensed money lenders; and fourth, against members of syndicates, for example, global match-fixing syndicates.
A more comprehensive list of the activities of a criminal nature are listed in the fourth schedule of the Act.
It is an important principle, as it prevents the abuse of process by an incompetent or corrupt Government.
However, I accept that the argument that this law is needed in unique circumstances, where witnesses are unwilling to testify because of the fear of harm to themselves or to their loved ones.

Indeed, when this Bill was up for renewal in 2009, I had supported the renewal of the Bill and at that session, I had given an account of a criminal case that I did in 1990, when I was asked to interview a secret society member who was charged in Court for murder.

However, 15 years later, the question before Members of this House is whether the current state of criminal activities in Singapore would still warrant renewal of the Act, after almost 70 years since the Act was first introduced.
Is this law still relevant to Singapore, in this day and age?
Is it still necessary in maintaining law and order?
For most Members of this House, we have limited knowledge of the state of criminal activities, save for what was reported in the media or by the Police.
For example, in February 2021, Minister for Home Affairs Mr Shanmugam, in reply to a PQ, said that the secret society situation in Singapore is under control.
He said there was one case involving weapons last year, down from 12 in 2016.

On 5 July 2021, the Minister said in a reply to another PQ, that notwithstanding that the secret society situation remains under control, the participation of youths in secret societies remain a concern.
That is why we invest significant resources to educate and engage youths, to deter them from joining secret societies.
And this was a 40% decrease, from the 2,642 cases reported during the same period in 2019.
Now, they arrest about 3,000 to 3,500 per year.
Furthermore, the death penalty is a key part of our system and approach to deal with drug traffickers.

Thus the question is, if the secret society situation in Singapore is under control, if the cases involving unlicensed moneylending has come down by 40%, if the number of drugs abusers have also come down drastically since the 1990s, is there still justification for this law to be extended?
However, in every criminal case, there will always be a risk of retribution, whether by secret society members or by simple criminals.
The question is, how can we balance the interests of an individual, to the right of due process, versus the right of members of public, to a peaceful and safe living environment in Singapore?
According to the Global Peace Index, the safest Asian country to visit is Singapore, followed by Japan and Malaysia.
It was reported that this countries have low levels of violence, crime and conflict, and high levels of stability and security.
The country that tops the list of safest countries in the world, not just in Asia.
So, the country that tops the list of safest countries in the world in 2024, is Iceland, followed by Denmark, Austria and New Zealand.
So, my question to the Minister of State is whether these countries also have similar legislation that allows them to detain criminals without trial?
How did they maintain their record of being safe countries to visit?
And how did they deal with the criminal activities that Singapore is so concerned with?
If the Minister is able to make out a compelling case, then I will be happy to support the extension.

The Public Prosecutor, who is also the Attorney-General, enjoys security of tenure under the Constitution, and the public prosecutor is free to disagree with the Police, or even a Minister, and still enjoys the security of tenure.

We are having the best judicial minds, reviewing the Minister's basis for the detention or supervision order, and challenging the decision of the Police in requesting for such detention or supervision order.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Please allow me to address some points they have raised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Assoc Prof Razwana Begum asked if we still require the Act for the maintenance of law and order in today's Singapore, given that crimes involving drugs, unlicensed moneylending and secret societies are now under control.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I have explained this in my opening speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Act has been an integral part of our arsenal and complements our existing laws.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We must not be complacent, even if the secret society situation in Singapore is under control.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Lim also asked about other countries in the world which have topped the Global Peace Index and wondered if they have similar legislation as ours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I must emphasise that our laws are unique to our background and our circumstances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I have explained how the powers under the Act came about, and how the Act has served us well in maintaining public safety, peace and good order.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We have studied the gang situation in other countries that do not have a similar legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For instance, New Zealand continues to be plagued by gangs and gang-related crimes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Economist reported that New Zealand had one of the world's highest gang membership rates in 2018.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Without the Act, we face a real risk of an uncontrolled gang situation and a rise in violent and other serious crimes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We cannot afford to have this in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Dennis Tan has asked for various statistics on how the Act has been used in the past.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: MHA does not generally release information about the use of the Act as we need to balance the call for transparency against the need to prevent prejudice to investigations and to keep witnesses safe.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Tan also asked about the use of technology in Police enforcement methods.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In this regard, the use of Police cameras has greatly assisted the Police's enforcement efforts, especially in unlicensed moneylending cases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Police will continue to leverage technology as a key strategy in its enforcement approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: However, as we have emphasised, the Act is an instrument of last resort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Murali Pillai and Assoc Prof Razwana raised concerns on the involvement of youths in secret societies and asked if the Police could take more preventive measures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Murali also asked if powers of detention could be used on recruiters of secret society members, who are not personally involved in violent activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I will first say that we share the same concerns about youths' involvement in gangs and agree that their recruitment into secret societies must be taken seriously.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Police adopts a two-pronged strategy of enforcement and prevention to address the problem of street gangs, particularly among youths.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Besides taking firm enforcement actions, Police routinely conduct community outreach programmes and work with key partners to implement a range of diversionary and rehabilitative initiatives to educate the public on the dangers of joining gangs; and to discourage, deter and detect youth involvement in gangs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Some of these partners include other Government agencies, such as MSF, MOE and Social Service Agencies such as Family Service Centres.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Police's educational efforts include organising talks at schools, arranging prison visits for wayward youths, their parents and guardians and promoting programmes, like the Streetwise Programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We hope that these programmes will raise awareness and prevent youths from becoming involved in gang activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: When it comes to enforcement, the Ministry views recruitment of youths into gangs as particularly aggravating as this perpetuates the gangland lawlessness, while corrupting our youths.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I will now address questions raised by Members relating to the operational aspects of the Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Ng asked about the nature of obligations imposed on a supervisee, who is under a PSO.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The obligations that Minister may impose can be found in Rule 3 of the Criminal Law (Obligations on Person Subject to Supervision) Rules 2018.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These obligations include requiring the supervisee to reside at a specified place, curfews; restrictions on where a supervisee may enter, restrictions on who the supervisee may communicate with, amongst others.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We review the Rules and obligations from time to time, to ensure that they remain relevant and effective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Ng also raised a few queries concerning the second and third types of Advisory Committees that review detention cases at least annually.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These two Advisory Committees comprise senior lawyers and prominent private citizens with extensive relevant experience and knowledge in areas, such as the criminal justice system and rehabilitation of ex-convicts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As to Mr Ng's question on what support is provided to these two Advisory Committees to aid them in reviewing existing DOs, they have access to all relevant information including: first, the nature and gravity of offences committed; second, the detainee’s criminal antecedents; third, the detainee's conduct and response towards Prisons' rehabilitation programme; fourth, the detainee’s likelihood of re-offending and continuing to pose a threat to safety and security; and last, the detainee's re-integration plans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As Mr Gan Thiam Poh has rightly pointed out, this system of Advisory Committees being supported by professionals has worked well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Ng also asked whether these two Advisory Committees have exercised their powers under section 40 of the Act to summon and examine a witness, or to compel the production of documents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai has suggested additional safeguards to the Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The current safeguards are carefully considered and we have explained several times why this structure works for us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We have explained why MHA, acting with the Minister and with the advisory structures, is the best structure and has kept law and order.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: It seems that they are not able to point to any abuse of the system – Singapore is ranked number one in law and order.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I think what is key, is let us stop pursuing theory and just ask whether it has worked or has not worked for us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If it has worked and there are no obvious flaws then we must ask, what we are trying to change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: On the issue of the President: the responsibility for law and order lies with the Government, not the President.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The President is there in specific respects, as identified in the Constitution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Beyond that, the President has no executive power, and if something goes wrong with law and order, it is the Government that is accountable to the people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We have an Executive that answers to Parliament.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In specific circumstances, the President has powers to veto, but law and order is an Executive responsibility, not the President's responsibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Therefore, we did not agree with this suggestion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: However, they may choose to be represented by any lawyer of their choice or seek pro bono representation under schemes that may be available to them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I now turn to Mr Ng and Assoc Prof Razwana's queries regarding the rehabilitative aspects of the detention regime, in particular, the programmes that are in place for detainees while in Prison.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Detainees are housed in the various institutions in Changi Prison Complex, based on their security risks and rehabilitative needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Prison works closely with every detainee to understand each detainee's rehabilitative needs, before placing them on programmes to target specific behavioural and offending needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Prison engages different agencies to provide a range of programmes to detainees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Detainees are also given access to vocational training, religious counselling and education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Where required, detainees undergo the gang renunciation programme or psychological-based correctional programmes to increase their self-awareness and equip them with pro-social skills to change their offending ways.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Family support is also important in a detainee's rehabilitation journey.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As such, detainees are encouraged to maintain a close relationship with their family members through letters and visits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Prison also engages specialised family services agencies to deliver structured family programmes that seek to address transitional issues for detainees and their families, with the view of helping detainees build skills and confidence to maintain ties and build stronger relationships with their family members.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: With respect, it is not meaningful to make such a comparison, as the two regimes are complementary to each other.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For instance, an individual may be detained on one occasion and be prosecuted in Court for other offences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The point I want to make is that Prison takes the rehabilitation of every detainee seriously – each detainee undergoes programmes customised to his profile and needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I now turn to the final issue, as raised by Mr Murali.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: He also asked about the relevance of Parts 2, 3 and 4 of the Act; and whether these provisions should be ported over to other legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: MHA is certainly cognisant that the Act consists of these provisions and had, in the course of preparing for this Bill, satisfied ourselves that they remain relevant and necessary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We will continue to review these provisions and propose changes, if necessary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: And I want to also mention about a quote, where Mr Dennis Tan has quoted the Minister for Home Affairs in 1989, and has asked when the Government would be ready to do away with the Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai also touched on this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We have to recognise that each time the Act comes up for renewal, we must allow the Government of the day to consider the circumstances and current conditions; and come to the assessment of what is in the best interest of Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We should not bind future governments in its assessment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Once again, I thank Members for supporting the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I think the Minister of State actually mentioned that some of these information that I have sought, he said that it is not available.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This Act puts the Members of the House in a very special position to come together every five years to debate and decide on the extension.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: So, can I humbly request that the Ministry consider providing such information on a confidential basis, just to the Members of the House, for the purpose of the debate?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I believe I did ask for the Minister of State to clarify, whether in the past five years, whether there have been instances where the Public Prosecutor withheld consent or raised concerns when the Ministry sought to make an order.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Is the Minister of State able to address this question?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Like what I shared earlier, on why we are not able to share the details, I am not sure whether Member is aware, but the issue of gangs, secret societies, transnational crime is something that is very complex and deep.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, we need to be very careful about what we share.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: But I want to assure the Member that we have Singapore's interest at heart.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, it is something that I want to assure Members about.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We have shared information with the public, as I shared during the SPS Annual Reports.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The other aspect is about whether the Public Prosecutor has had reservation or some differences of opinion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Like what I shared earlier, it is a process where we put up to the different Advisory Committee as well as the Prosecutor, and it is a process; upon which the Prosecutor may ask us for further details and clarification, which we have done so in the past.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have a few further clarifications to make.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I ask the Minister of State whether our safeguards are really out of the ordinary?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because, for example, when we asked for the condition, or the requirement, that a sitting judge be part of the Advisory Committee and this condition to be codified in the Act, this is something that the Government is currently already practicing, as what the Minister of State has said and what I have read about the Bill recently.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is already something being practised, so what is the problem of codifying it in the Act itself?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: My second question is, putting in another requirement for this Bill that the President can act in his discretion is something that is also under the ISA, which carries the same draconian power to detain an individual without trial.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, since the ISA also has this condition, that the President can act in his discretion, why can this condition not be also put into this CLTPA Bill?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
